idiom_name: value-semantic structs/enums + repository protocol + mapping extensions over Core Data/SwiftData or GRDB types
implementation_notes: Swift prefers structures and enumerations for the model, so the domain is plain structs and enums conforming to Sendable, with repository protocols (async, often implemented by an actor) as the boundary; the data model is whatever the persistence framework insists on - NSManagedObject subclasses in Core Data, @Model classes in SwiftData, or FetchableRecord/PersistableRecord structs in GRDB - and mapping extensions (func toDomain() -> Order, func toManagedObject(in:) -> OrderEntity) replace the Mapper class. Because structs cannot be mutated field by field from outside, rehydration must go through an initialiser, which is exactly the property the pattern wants; what must be avoided is storing or passing the framework's class instances (managed objects, @Model instances) through the domain layer.
pitfalls: Core Data identity and faults: NSManagedObject instances are classes with object identity, lazy faults and a context, so passing one into the domain reintroduces context-bound objects and implicit queries; map to structs at the repository boundary instead.

@Model/SwiftData couples schema to the class: macro-annotated types cannot be the domain model without leaking the framework, and @Query/ModelContext in views pulls persistence into the presentation layer.

Predicates and fetches encode rules in the data layer: a business rule implemented in a fetch predicate is not enforced when an object is created in memory, so invariants must be re-checked after rehydration.
Value semantics hide mapping errors: an initialiser that silently accepts default/optional values turns a mis-mapped column into a valid-looking but wrong domain object.
